 Election Live: Three Virginia races will set the tone tonight 
 This is where we’ll be commenting on the election through the day and the results once they come in. 
 by 
 Dwayne Yancey 
 November 3, 2026 November 3, 2026

 Welcome to our running updates on the 2026 election. This is where we’ll be posting updates during the day and then analyzing the returns after the polls close. 
 Polls open at 6 a.m., close at 7 p.m. Once the polls close, we’ll have live results from the Virginia Department of Elections on cardinalnews.org. 
 Want text alerts on election results? Sign up here. 
 Got photos from polling locations today? You can share them at dwayne@cardinalnews.org . Please let me know who you are and where the photo was taken . 
 Want more information about who’s on the ballot? See our  Voter Guide. 
 If you’re really into politics, sign up for our weekly political newsletter, West of the Capital:
 Sign up 
 5:06 p.m.: Speaker Johnson will be watching three Virginia races closely
 CNN reports that House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana, will be watching three Virginia races closely to get a sense of how the night will go: the 1st, 2nd, and 5th districts, all held now by Republicans. Losing the 2nd (held by Jen Kiggans) would be bad, but not may not indicate a blue wave. Losing the 1st (held by Rob Wittman) would. And if Republicans lose the 5th (held by John McGuire): “If we lose John McGuire’s district in Virginia 5, then we are in for a bloodbath,” an unnamed Republican told CNN.
 A look at the races House Speaker Mike Johnson and his team will be tracking closely as they try to get a read of the tea leaves early in the night
“If we lose John McGuire’s district in Virginia 5, then we are in for a bloodbath” a GOP operative said https://t.co/4ezjjKjTkH 
— Annie Grayer (@AnnieGrayerCNN) November 3, 2026 
 4:56 p.m.: Fairfax County and Prince William County voting at higher rates than last year
 Fairfax County reports that as of 3 p.m., 47.49% of its voters had cast ballots (either today or through early voting). That’s up from 44.0% at 3 p.m. in last year’s governor’s race.
 Prince William County also reports turnout higher today than last year.
 This is akin to the old George Carlin joke about sportscasters: “And here’s a partial score, Philadelphia 3.” Without knowing more about other localities, we can form a complete picture but it does appear that these Northern Virginia localities (both of which typically vote Democratic) are going to come in higher than last year’s turnout. That’s good news for Democrat Mark Warner in the Senate race and the three constitutional amendments, but doesn’t give us any insight into the most contested congressional races, which aren’t in Northern Virginia. 
 The late day push has begun! More than 8K PWC voters cast a ballot in the last hour. Through 4 PM, ~65K PWC voters have cast Election Day ballots, up 5.2% compared to 2025. Early/mail voting are up 16% from 2025 and ballots are still being mailed and dropped off today.
— Prince William County Office of Elections (@PWCVotes) November 3, 2026 
 2:13 p.m.: Data site says Virginia Democrats are voting at higher rate than Republicans
 G. Elliott Morris, author of “Strength in Numbers” and newsletter by the same name, reports that Democrats are voting at a rate 9-10 percentage points higher than Republicans across Virginia today. He draws on data collected by State Navigate (run by Virginia Tech grad Chaz Nuttycombe). This chart doesn’t appear to have every locality in Virginia, but notably it shows a high turnout rate in Henrico County, a Democratic-voting locality that’s home to Shannon Taylor, who is challenging Republican incumbent Rob Wittman. This ought to be good news for her, although I’d like to see more localities to draw firmer conclusions. Notice that James City County, another locality Taylor will need, is voting at a lower rate.
 Fresh E-Day turnout data in VA, courtesy of State Navigate, implies Dem **E Day voters** are voting at a rate about 9-10 percentage points higher than Republicans. This is on top of the Democratic lead in engaging early voters in the state. https://t.co/j4thzx0YRZ pic.twitter.com/J6JU1VfeQV 
— G Elliott Morris (@gelliottmorris) November 3, 2026 
 1 p.m.: Obama robocall for Macy pushes data center moratorium
 Former President Barack Obama has recorded a robocall for Beth Macy, the Democratic candidate in the 6th District who is challenging Republican incumbent Ben Cline. It emphasizes her support for a data center moratorium, according to CNN , which obtained a recording of the call.
 “If you send her to Congress, she’ll fight to lower everyday costs, make healthcare more affordable, and pass a moratorium on data centers,” Obama says in the recording, according to CNN.
 Cardinal’s Elizabeth Beyer wrote earlier this fall about where both candidates stand on data centers. Cline has indicated support for a “pause” but Macy has made a moratorium more central to her campaign.
 12:47 p.m.: Fairfax County turnout trending higher than last year
 We have our first turnout report. It’s from 9 a.m., so we’re looking back in time several hours. Fairfax County reports that as of that hour, 6.19% of its registered voters had cast ballots today, while 27.9% had voted early. That’s a total turnout as of 9 a.m. of 34.09%.
 For comparison, at that point a year ago, 6.2% of Fairfax County voters had voted that day while 23.9% had voted early, for a total turnout of 30.1%. Fairfax County last year eventually posted a final turnout of 55%, just a shade higher than the statewide turnout of 54.31%.
 If those trends hold, the Fairfax numbers suggest Virginia’s totall turnout will come in higher than last year’s governor’s race. Of course, that ultimately depends on turnout in 132 other localities and we saw that the early voting turnout in many rural localities has lagged.
 11:56 a.m.: Dueling Republican sample ballots in Lynchburg
 Lynchburg has two rival Republican slates for city council, both running as independents after the state party voided the results of the party-run process that attempted to nominate council candidates. Sometimes it seems those two slates dislike each other more than they dislike the Democratic slate. Today Lynchburg voters may see two different sample ballots claiming to be the Republican sample ballot. Lynchburg council member Chris Faraldi (who is supporting the Team Lynchburg slate) shares these photos:
 This is the sample ballot for the Team Lynchburg slate: Chris Bowell, Stephanie Reed, Larry Taylor. Photo courtesy of Chris Faraldi.

 8:53 a.m.: Both McGuire and Perriello are out at the polls today
 John McGuire with supporters in Goochland County early Tuesday morning. Courtesy of McGuire. 
 The 5th Congressional District is one we’ll be keeping special tabs on today. Forecasters can’t agree on how it will go: Cook Political Report has it leans Republican, Sabato’s Crystal Ball has it leans Democratic. The only thing we know for sure is that it likely will be close. 
 Both candidates were up and at ’em early this morning, Republican incumbent John McGuire in Goochland County, Democratic challenge Tom Perriello in Halifax County. Here are some photos they posted.
 My Monday column looked at the disparities in early voting in the district, with Democratic localities having a heavy early vote while many Republican localities lagged. McGuire will want and need a big day-of turnout today.
 Tom Perriello greets an early morning voter in Halifax County. Courtesy of Perriello. 
 6 a.m.: The polls are now open
 And so it begins. If you have photos from your polling place (signs, lines, no lines, whatever), please share them at dwayne@cardinalnews.org and let me know what precinct they’re from.\
 Takis Karantonis of the Arlington County Board (no board of supervisors there, just board) posts this cool video of a polling place opening:
 The polls are now open #ArlingtonVA #Virginia ! #VoteBLUE pic.twitter.com/F8wVb1tnX9 
— Takis Karantonis (@TakisKarantonis) November 3, 2026 
 4 a.m.: The early voting was ‘lumpy’ in ways that appear to favor Democrats (but not all of them)
 Virginia’s current congressional districts, approved in late 2021. Courtesy of Twotwofourtysix. 
 Story continues below 
 The only thing we know for certain is that at least 1,634,190 Virginians have voted early. I say “at least” because, while the in-person early voting concluded Saturday, mail ballots are still arriving (and under Virginia law, can still be counted if they are properly postmarked and arrive by Friday). That’s 13.9% more early votes than we had in last year’s governor’s race, but we won’t know until the election is over whether that represents an actual increase in voting or whether one or both parties simply shifted voters from day-of voting to early voting. If it’s an actual increase, then we’re looking at turnout north of last year’s 54.13% of registered voters. The record in Virginia for a congressional midterm is 59.15%. That was in 2018, during Donald Trump’s first term.
 The early voting is “lumpy,” meaning it’s higher in some places than others. I addressed that in a column Monday: The general theme is that early voting in some Democratic localities is running closer to their 2024 levels while Republican localities are lagging. Southwest Virginia, in particular, is running well behind its 2024 levels:
 This map shows how close each locality came in the 2026 early voting to matching its early voting in the 2024 presidential election. The greener a locality is, the closer it came to the presidential year early vote; the brown localities came in lower.
 My column Monday went into more details, but for those who just want the highlights: The voter drop-off in Southwest Virginia is not good for the “no” side on the constitutional amendments. The “no” side will need a big day-of turnout there to make up for that.
 The turnout patterns in the 1st and 2nd congressional districts are inconclusive to my eye and aren’t helpful to Democrats in the 6th. The key place to watch is the 5th District, where Democrat Tom Perriello is challenging Republican John McGuire. 
 You’ll notice the particularly high voting levels in the Democratic strongholds: Charlottesville, Danville, Albemarle County. Think of this in terms of a tornado watch. A tornado watch doesn’t mean there’s a tornado, just that conditions exist for one to form. Same here: This doesn’t mean there’s a Democratic upset in the making, but it does mean conditions exist. The key is how heavy the day-of voting will be in that district. That’s one of many things we’ll be watching today.
